newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke says budget was not cynical.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke says budget was not cynical.

text.p: UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said his 1997/98 budget had not been cynical and he did not object to it being described as dull and cautious.
"They said that about my budget last year and actually the economy hasn't looked back since," he said in an interview with GMTV.
He acknowledged that the budget contained few surprises but added: "The fact is it's good economic policy."
Responding to the opposition Labour party's charge that the Conservatives had made 22 tax rises since the last election, Clarke said he had made around 22 tax reductions as well.
Labour's calculations included the four increases in tobacco tax, which the opposition had supported.
Asked if the average British family was now more heavily taxed, directly and indirectly, than in 1991, Clarke replied: "I'm not sure."
"People who exchange figures on that, you'll find, will give you a bewildering series of slightly jokey figures. What I will say is the average man is certainly better off."
"Some of his taxes have gone down, some have gone up," Clarke added. "The balance is favourable. In particular, the spending power of the ordinary population is higher."

Asked if the budget had been a cynical attempt to win votes, the chancellor said: "It's certainly not cynical...I certainly wanted to do the best for the economy and that's why people are calling it dull."
